options.text: A measurement of a service's behaviour, ideally from the user's perspective
options.note: Right. For example, how fast a page loads.

options.text: A contract with penalties for downtime
options.note: That describes an SLA.

options.text: A target percentage the team commits to
options.note: That's an SLO.

options.text: A type of Prometheus metric
options.note: The metric types are counter, gauge, histogram and summary.

explanation: SLI, or service level indicator, represents a measurement of a service's behaviour. A good SLI measures the service from the perspective of its users.
hint: I is for indicator: a measurement.

options.text: A target for one or more SLIs, tied to business value and used to communicate reliability
options.note: Right. For example, 95% of requests within 300 ms.

options.text: The raw measurement of request latency
options.note: That's the SLI.

options.text: A legal agreement with customers
options.note: That's an SLA.

options.text: A Prometheus recording rule
options.note: Recording rules can help compute SLIs, but they aren't SLOs.

explanation: SLO, or service level objective, communicates reliability to an organisation or other teams by attaching one or more SLIs to business value.
hint: O is for objective: a target.

stem: Which describes an SLA, in common industry usage?

options.text: An agreement, often contractual, with consequences such as credits if the promised level isn't met
options.note: Right. The cited docs don't define SLA, so this is general usage.

options.text: An internal measurement of error rate
options.note: That's an SLI.

options.text: An internal engineering target
options.note: That's an SLO. An SLA is the external promise.

options.text: An Alertmanager silence
options.note: Unrelated.

explanation: SLA, or service level agreement, is the general industry term for an external promise with consequences. The cited official docs define SLI and SLO but not SLA.

stem: Your SLA promises 99.5% availability. How should your internal SLO compare?

options.text: Stricter, such as 99.9%, so you're alerted before the SLA is breached
options.note: Right. The margin gives time to react.

options.text: Looser, such as 99%, to avoid noisy alerts
options.note: Then you'd break the SLA before your SLO even complained.

options.text: Exactly the same, 99.5%
options.note: No margin. You'd only notice at the moment you owe credits.

options.text: SLOs and SLAs shouldn't be related
options.note: The SLO should protect the SLA.

explanation: SLAs are external promises with consequences. Keeping the internal objective stricter means problems surface before the promise is broken. (General practice, in our own words.)
hint: You want warning before you owe anything.

stem: Which is the best SLI for a web shop's checkout?

options.text: The fraction of checkout requests that succeed within 300 ms
options.note: Right. It measures what users experience.

options.text: CPU usage of the checkout servers
options.note: CPU is a cause-level signal. Users can suffer while CPU looks fine.

options.text: Number of pods running
options.note: Internal capacity, not user experience.

options.text: Disk free on the database host
options.note: Possibly a cause, not a user-facing measure.

explanation: A good SLI measures the service from the users' perspective. Prometheus alerting practice likewise says to alert on symptoms associated with end-user pain, such as latency and errors.

stem: The SLO is "95% of requests served within 300 ms". Using a classic histogram with a 0.3 bucket, which expression gives the SLI?

options.text: The rate of the `le="0.3"` bucket divided by the rate of `_count`, both summed by job
options.note: Right. That's the fraction of requests at or under 300 ms.

options.text: `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)`
options.note: That gives the 95th percentile latency, not the fraction under 300 ms. It's useful, but it's a different question.

options.text: The rate of `_sum` divided by the rate of `_count`
options.note: That's the average duration.

options.text: The rate of the `le="+Inf"` bucket alone
options.note: That counts all requests, with no threshold.

explanation: The histograms page shows this expression for the 95%-within-300ms SLO: sum by (job) of rate(..._bucket{le="0.3"}[5m]) divided by sum by (job) of rate(..._count[5m]).
hint: Good events divided by all events.

stem: Your classic histogram has buckets at 0.25 and 0.5 but none at 0.3. What does the `le="0.3"` SLI expression return?

options.text: No result, because classic bucket selection doesn't interpolate
options.note: Right. You need a bucket boundary exactly at the threshold.

options.text: An interpolated estimate
options.note: Interpolation applies to histogram_quantile and histogram_fraction, not to selecting a bucket label.

options.text: The value of the 0.25 bucket
options.note: The label value must match exactly.

options.text: An error message
options.note: It quietly returns nothing.

explanation: The histograms page notes that the expression strictly requires a bucket boundary at 0.3. Without one, no interpolation is applied and no result is returned.
hint: A label matcher matches exact values.

stem: Why do the Prometheus docs suggest native histograms make changing an SLO threshold easier?

options.text: `histogram_fraction` can estimate the fraction under any threshold, with no fixed bucket needed at that value
options.note: Right. Changing the threshold doesn't mean changing instrumentation.

options.text: Native histograms store every raw observation
options.note: They still use buckets, just dynamic exponential ones.

options.text: Native histograms automatically create SLO alerts
options.note: No automatic alerts are created.

options.text: Classic histograms can't be used for SLOs
options.note: They can, if a bucket boundary sits at the threshold.

explanation: With native histograms, histogram_fraction(0, 0.3, ...) estimates the fraction by interpolation. You gain the freedom to change range boundaries at will, which helps if your SLO changes.
hint: Recall histogram_fraction from the histograms topic.

stem: With an SLO of 99% of requests succeeding, what is the error budget?

options.text: 1% of requests may fail before the SLO is missed
options.note: Right. The budget is the gap between 100% and the target.

options.text: 99% of requests may fail
options.note: That inverts it.

options.text: Zero failures allowed
options.note: That would be a 100% target.

options.text: The money set aside for SLA credits
options.note: The term is about allowed unreliability, not money.

explanation: An error budget, a general industry term explained in our own words, is the amount of unreliability an SLO allows: 100% minus the target.

stem: Which alert best follows SLO-based, symptom-first alerting?

options.text: The fraction of requests under 300 ms has been below 0.95 for 10 minutes
options.note: Right. A user-facing symptom, with slack for blips.

options.text: Any single pod restarted
options.note: That's a cause, and often no user notices.

options.text: CPU above 80% on any node
options.note: That's a cause-level signal.

options.text: Every 5xx error triggers a page
options.note: There's no slack for small blips. That's noisy.

explanation: Prometheus alerting practice: alert on symptoms associated with end-user pain, such as latency and errors, as high in the stack as possible, and allow slack for small blips.
